title: Spectral Theorem
body:
**Spectral theorem (real case):** a matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable exactly when it is
symmetric. For $A^T = A$,

$$
A = QDQ^T, \qquad Q^{-1} = Q^T
$$

with $D$ real diagonal holding the eigenvalues and $Q$ an [[Orthonormal Basis|orthogonal matrix]]
whose columns are the eigenvectors.

[[Diagonalization]] covers $A = PDP^{-1}$ in general, where $P$ can be any invertible
matrix and might not exist at all. This note is about what symmetry buys, which is three things
that ordinary diagonalization does not give you:

1. **The eigenvalues are real.** No complex case to handle, so no rotation component.
2. **The eigenvectors are orthogonal**, and can be scaled to orthonormal. Eigenvectors from
   *distinct* eigenvalues are orthogonal automatically; a repeated eigenvalue gives an eigenspace
   you run [[Gram-Schmidt]] inside.
3. **It never fails.** Every symmetric matrix is diagonalizable, defective ones included in the
   general theory but excluded here. Repeated eigenvalues always have full-dimensional
   eigenspaces.

The payoff on the arithmetic: $P^{-1}$ becomes $Q^T$, so there is no inverse to compute anywhere,
and $A^k = QD^kQ^T$ is free.

## The spectral decomposition

Writing $A = QDQ^T$ out column by column gives the form the rest of the course uses:

$$
A = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i\, \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T
$$

Each $\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T$ is a rank-one [[Projection]] onto one eigenvector direction, so
**a symmetric matrix is a weighted sum of projections**. Applying $A$ means: project onto each
eigendirection, scale by $\lambda_i$, add the pieces back. Drop the small $\lambda_i$ and you have
an approximation, which is [[Low-Rank Approximation]] in the symmetric case and the exact template
[[Singular Value Decomposition]] generalises to rectangular matrices.

## Why data science lives here

**The matrices that come out of data are symmetric almost by construction.** A covariance matrix
$\frac{1}{n-1}X_c^TX_c$ is symmetric, a Gram matrix $A^TA$ is symmetric, an adjacency matrix of an
undirected [[Graph]] is symmetric, a [[Quadratic Form]]'s matrix and a Hessian are symmetric. So
the theorem applies to nearly everything worth decomposing, and the guarantee of an orthogonal
eigenbasis is what lets [[Principal Component Analysis]] claim its components are uncorrelated
rather than merely different.

$A^TA$ is more than symmetric: it is positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are $\geq 0$ and
their square roots are the singular values of $A$. That sentence is the whole bridge from this
note to [[Singular Value Decomposition]].

## Worked example

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$\det(A - \lambda I) = (2-\lambda)^2 - 1$, so $\lambda = 3, 1$ (real, as promised). Eigenvectors
$\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}$, whose dot product is
zero without any effort on our part. Normalise:

$$
Q = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad
D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad A = QDQ^T
$$

Sanity checks from [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] still apply: trace $4 = 3+1$, determinant
$3 = 3\times 1$.

## Related

- [[Quadratic Form]]: definiteness is just the sign of the $\lambda_i$

- [[Principal Component Analysis]]: this theorem applied to a covariance matrix
